docs.title: Humble is primary; Foxy is kept alive through backports, not dual-distro code
docs.text:
All Pilsbot repositories get a humble and a foxy branch. Repositories that used foxy-devel rename it to foxy. Repositories that used main/master branch both lines from there, and later move main/master forward to humble. New work lands on the Humble line. Substantial improvements that do not depend on the distro are cherry-picked to the Foxy line: ROS-free cores, bug fixes, the frame re-root, and the robot profile. The ros2_control adapters and launch-API changes stay Humble-only.

We rejected making every package build on both distros (#if on ros2_control versions). The hardware and controller APIs changed completely between Foxy and Humble, so this would roughly double the work in the code that is riskiest to change. Backporting stays cheap because the logic worth backporting is deliberately kept free of ROS.

Only our own code is ported. Third-party packages are consumed as their upstream or the Humble binaries provide them.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: • A backport can only carry what Foxy can use. The robot profile's Foxy backport (ADR 0009) cannot carry the gamepad fields devices.joystick.device_id and device_name, because they exist for Humble's SDL-based joy_node. Foxy's joy_node opens a device path (/dev/input/js0), so that part of the profile differs between the lines.

docs.title: The robot reference point moves from the front axle to the rear axle centre
docs.text:
base_link used to be the front axle. The chassis and the OAK hung off the steering joint, so the camera's pose relative to base_link changed with every steering angle. This breaks the assumptions of visual SLAM and of the Ackermann planners. base_link now sits at the rear axle centre, with base_footprint on the ground below it. The odometry frame is renamed from odom_raw to odom.

The odometry estimator is deliberately left unchanged. Its front-axle pose is converted to the rear axle centre by a pure frame transform that uses the measured steering angle and the wheelbase. The transform is a ROS-free function in the controller core (acker_diff_core.cpp). The legacy-log converter uses a Python twin of it (pilsbot_log_tools/rear_axle.py), and both test files check the same hand-derived values, so live data and translated Kohlfahrt logs agree as long as those tests pass. Replacing the estimator with a bicycle model is a separate, later decision.

The controller publishes the result as odom → base_footprint, and the URDF root is base_footprint with base_link one wheel radius above it. The published twist is the same pure transform applied to velocities: the chassis yaws at the front-axle yaw rate plus the steering rate, which is differenced from consecutive steering measurements. It is deliberately not the no-slip bicycle constraint. Any lateral velocity it reports at the rear axle is the estimator's inconsistency made visible, not hidden.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Kohlfahrt logs recorded since Feb 2023 contain no /tf. A missing comma in log_kohl.launch.py merged it into /stereo/camera_info/tf. The converter rebuilds TF from the recorded /joint_states and /odom and from the current URDF, which it generates from the robot profile (ADR 0009). It ignores the recorded /robot_description and writes MCAP.
  • Because the converter uses the current URDF and wheelbase, a log converted again after the wheelbase is re-measured comes out different. Converted logs are derived data: keep the originals, and convert again after a change to the profile.
  • The wheelbase must be measured on the robot. The old values disagree: 0.67 in the controller config and about 0.68 in the URDF.
  • The odom origin stays where the estimator starts: the front axle's pose at reset. base_footprint therefore starts one wheelbase away from the origin rather than at it. It lies exactly behind the origin on the x axis only if the steering angle δ0 at reset is zero. Otherwise it starts at (−L·cos δ0, −L·sin δ0) with heading δ0, for wheelbase L.
  • The stock diff-drive fallback config estimates the front axle, so it labels its odometry front_axle and publishes no TF.

docs.title: The Jetson Nano runs two Humble containers: an L4T camera container and a stock stack container
docs.text:
The Nano is limited to L4T r32 (Ubuntu 18.04). The only Humble images that keep Jetson's hardware (GStreamer nvjpegdec/nvv4l2decoder, CUDA, TensorRT) are dusty-nv's dustynv/ros:humble-*-l4t-r32.7.1. They build ROS from source with gcc-8 and Python 3.6, and apt install ros-humble-* does not work in them. The official ros:humble (22.04) arm64 image has every binary package but no access to Jetson hardware. We use both:

  • Camera container (dustynv L4T): owns the OAK and its hardware-accelerated decoding, and the CSI camera (jetson_camera), which needs Jetson Argus. Only this container builds depthai from source.
  • Stack container (official ros:humble): ros2_control, the controllers, the driver, teleop, GNSS, localisation, navigation, foxglove_bridge, and recording, all from apt.

Both use CycloneDDS (RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=rmw_cyclonedds_cpp) with --network=host --ipc=host.

docs.title: Considered options
docs.text:
• Everything in the dustynv container: rejected. ros2_control, Nav2, and rtabmap would all need source builds on gcc-8 and Python 3.6, and nav2 and rtabmap have no confirmed working build there.
  • Everything in the official image: rejected. It loses the hardware decoding the camera driver depends on to stay fast.

docs.title: Transition
docs.text: The camera container stays on the existing, proven Foxy image (pilsbot/foxy-jetson, L4T, CycloneDDS) while the stack container moves to Humble. Foxy and Humble interoperate over DDS for the camera's message types. A Humble desktop on FastDDS received the Foxy camera streams at full rate (2026-11-26, see ADR 0004). Moving the camera container to the dustynv Humble image is a separate, later step and does not block the Humble port of the rest of the stack.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Full-resolution decoded frames are expensive to send between processes. Consumers of them should live in the camera container, ideally in the same process, unless measurements show the DDS copy is acceptable.
  • Open: rtabmap is meant to use the OAK's full widescreen colour resolution, and it may benefit from CUDA. Both point towards running it in the camera container, which would need a source build there. To be decided with measurements in M3/M4.
  • The Foxy line uses the same repos-file and devcontainer layout with the existing pilsbot/foxy-jetson image. The old foxy-jetson workspace branch, with its untracked gitlinks, is retired.

docs.title: We keep our own OAK camera node instead of depthai_ros_driver
docs.text: pilsbot_depthai keeps its own nodes (rgb_stereo_node, h265_node, mjpeg_node) and does not move to upstream depthai_ros_driver. The OAK encodes colour (1080p, ISP-scaled to 1280×720) and the mono pair as MJPEG on the camera. On the Nano these are decoded by a GStreamer pipeline (appsrc → [jpegparse] → nvjpegdec | nvv4l2decoder → nvvidconv → appsink), with software jpegdec/videoconvert as the fallback. Moving uncompressed frames over USB and handling them on the Nano's CPU cost too much. Getting hardware decoding to work took substantial effort, and upstream has no equivalent for the Nano.

docs.title: Verified state (2026-11-26, Nano on L4T R32.7.2, Foxy container)
docs.text:
Run as ros2 launch pilsbot_depthai mjpeg_node.launch.py nvdecoder:=nvv4l2decoder enable_raw_decode:=true from feature/h265-encoded-transport @ adc8a64:

  • nvv4l2decoder (not nvjpegdec) is the decoder in use. The NVIDIA GStreamer elements are provided by --runtime=nvidia; copying jetson_multimedia_api into the image is not needed.
  • Colour 1280×720 MJPEG at 30 fps (about 3.3 MB/s), each mono stream 400p at 15 fps (about 0.39 MB/s), decoded colour Image at about 27 fps.
  • The node uses about a third of one CPU core while idle, rising to about half a core with a subscriber on the decoded image. The rest of the Nano stays about 85% idle.
  • A Humble desktop (FastDDS, Wi-Fi) receives the streams from the Foxy/CycloneDDS container at full rate.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Only one process can open the OAK. Depth, encoders, and any on-camera neural network must share this node's pipeline.
  • nvjpegdec cannot share a process with code that uses the system libjpeg, which includes OpenCV's image decoding (see commit f40023b). Whether this also applies to the nvv4l2decoder path in use has not been checked, so composing OpenCV-heavy consumers into the decoder's process stays an open question.
  • The GStreamer pipeline is known to be brittle. Its build and runtime dependencies must be scripted in the camera container's Dockerfile, not just remembered.
  • The foxy-devel → foxy/humble branches must absorb feature/h265-encoded-transport, and all nodes must move to the Humble-era depthai-core API (CameraBoardSocket::CAM_A/B/C).

docs.title: Sidewalk segmentation runs on the OAK's neural accelerator first
docs.text: The segmentation network for the drivability map runs on the OAK-D Lite's Myriad X, inside the camera node's pipeline. This leaves the Nano's CPU and GPU free for SLAM and control. TensorRT on the Nano, in the camera container, is the fallback if the Myriad X proves too slow or the model needs unsupported layers. Picking the model is still open.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Models are limited to what OpenVINO can compile to a Myriad X blob (FP16, restricted op set), so they will be small mobile-sized networks.
  • Training images extracted from Kohlfahrt logs must be preprocessed exactly as the camera preprocesses the network's input. Recorded frames are MJPEG-compressed, while the on-camera network sees uncompressed ISP frames.

docs.title: Prefer ROS 2 standards that outlive Humble over custom equivalents
docs.text:
Where Humble offers a standard mechanism that persists in later distros, Pilsbot adopts it, even when this changes our own topics or recorded data. Custom code that only re-implements such a mechanism is removed, not ported.

First application: the custom pilsbot_sensor_broadcaster is removed. The upstream joint_state_broadcaster publishes the hoverboard and Head MCU <sensor> state interfaces on /dynamic_joint_states (control_msgs/DynamicJointState, verified with Humble 2.54 and mock hardware on 2026-11-26).

docs.title: Considered options
docs.text: • Port the custom broadcaster and keep /hoverboard_api and /head_mcu: rejected. It would keep a whole controller to maintain on every distro only to preserve topic names.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• New recordings contain /dynamic_joint_states instead of /hoverboard_api (pilsbot_driver_msgs/HoverboardAPISensors) and /head_mcu (pilsbot_driver_msgs/SteeringAxleSensorsStamped).
  • The legacy-log converter (ADR 0002) also maps those two legacy topics to /dynamic_joint_states, so datasets see one format across old and new logs.
  • The steering calibration script also reads the Head MCU values from /dynamic_joint_states, so it works while the ros2_control driver owns the Head MCU. The standalone head_mcu_node keeps publishing /head_mcu for calibration without the driver.

docs.title: Known exceptions
docs.text:
These forks predate this decision and are kept for now, because no standard covers them yet or they still need replacing:

  • ds4drv and ds4_driver: PS4 gamepad drivers without Humble binaries.
  • teleop_acker_joy: Ackermann teleop from a gamepad. teleop_twist_joy publishes only Twist. The workspace uses its foxy branch, because its GitHub humble branch is still the old upstream.
  • rqt_robot_steering (humble branch): the upstream plugin remapped to Ackermann commands.
  • The copies of diff_drive_controller's speed_limiter and odometry inside pils_control. Replacing them with the upstream classes is a planned clean-up.

A new fork needs the same justification: say which standard is missing or insufficient.

docs.title: The hardware starts inactive, and a hardware activator keeps it active
docs.text: Humble's ros2_control_node aborts when a hardware component fails to activate at startup ("Failed to set the initial state of the component"). On Foxy a missing hoverboard or Head MCU cost only driving. On Humble it took teleop, GNSS, lighting, Foxglove, and recording down with it. So the controller manager now starts PilsbotSystem inactive (hardware_components_initial_state.inactive), and the spawners load both controllers with --inactive. The hardware activator (pilsbot_driver's hardware_activator) brings them into operation. Every 5 s it asks the controller manager for the hardware's state. If the hardware is not active, it activates it. Once the hardware is active, it configures and activates any controller that is not. It does this at startup and again whenever the hardware drops out, and it logs a still-failing activation about once a minute. Each service call has a deadline (call_timeout, 30 s), so a hung or restarted controller manager cannot block it for good. It gives up only when the hardware is finalized, because that state cannot be left without restarting the controller manager.

docs.title: Considered options
docs.text:
• Respawn ros2_control_node until the devices answer: rejected. Every respawn would also restart the controllers and lose the odometry, and it would hide the cause in a restart loop. Supervision of the controller manager itself is the systemd service's job (ADR 0011).
  • Make activation always succeed and report missing devices later: rejected. The controller would then run on interfaces with no device behind them, and the activator would have nothing to act on.

docs.title: Fault handling
docs.text:
The activator only handles lifecycle failures. Faults while the hardware is active stay inside the driver and the controller, so they never cost an activation cycle:

Fault Driver Controller Hoverboard silent for 1 s NaN steering angle, power toggle requested (ADR 0008), read() OK halts the wheels Implausible hoverboard sample (EMI) sample dropped, last plausible speeds kept, read() OK carries on Serial read error NaN steering angle for that cycle, read() OK halts the wheels for that cycle Head MCU lost NaN steering angle and endstops at once, one reconnect attempt per second until it is back, read() OK halts the wheels Device missing at activation activation fails after its retries stays inactive; the activator retries

"Halts the wheels" means the controller writes 0 to both wheel commands and restarts its ramp and steering loop. When valid data returns, it ramps up from standstill. It does not resume at the speed it had before the fault.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The hardware and the controllers come up at least one activator period (5 s) after the launch, not with it. /odom and /joint_states start late too.
  • read() and write() return OK without touching anything until on_activate succeeded, because Humble calls them on inactive hardware as well.
  • Humble handles a read() or write() error with on_error and leaves the hardware unconfigured without on_deactivate. The driver therefore closes its ports and joins the Head MCU thread in on_error and on_cleanup too, so the next activation leaks nothing.
  • read() and write() return ERROR only when the hoverboard port is closed while the hardware is active, which only a re-activation can fix. A silent device is deliberately not an error, because the power toggle and the Head MCU reconnect need the hardware to stay active.

docs.title: The hoverboard's power button is pressed blind, on silence and on clean shutdown only
docs.text:
The hoverboard has a single power button and reports nothing about its power state except that it sends data while it is on. The Head MCU presses the button for the driver (a power toggle): pin high for 0.5 s, low for 0.5 s. Each toggle switches the hoverboard on or off, and whether it is on can only be inferred from whether its data arrives. The driver therefore toggles in exactly two situations:

  • Silence while active: no hoverboard data for 1 s. This is how the robot normally starts, because the hoverboard is off at boot. It also switches the hoverboard back on after it was switched off by hand. The Head MCU thread performs the toggle, so the ~1 s press does not block the control loop. Requests made during a press are dropped, so the driver toggles again only if the hoverboard is still silent afterwards.
  • Clean shutdown: on_deactivate, on_cleanup, or the driver's destructor, if the hoverboard sent data within the last second. This switches it off, as Foxy's stop() did.

It never toggles after on_error, after a failed activation, or because a port is missing. In those cases a toggle cannot help: the hoverboard's serial port exists whether it is on or not, and the activator retries within seconds (ADR 0007). A toggle there would only make the hoverboard flip state on every retry. While the Head MCU is lost, a pending request is dropped, because it could otherwise switch off a hoverboard that came back together with the Head MCU.

All of these durations are measured on the steady clock. The Nano has no RTC, and chrony, NTP, or GNSS step the system clock after boot. A forward step would fake a silence and switch the hoverboard off while driving.

docs.title: Considered options
docs.text:
• Track the power state in the driver and toggle only towards the wanted state: rejected. Without feedback the tracked state goes wrong the first time someone uses the button by hand, and from then on every toggle is the wrong one.
  • Toggle on every fault, as the first Humble port did through on_error: rejected. A single EMI spike cost about 7 s of drive and two toggles.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• A hoverboard that is on but whose data does not arrive (for example, a broken receive line) is toggled off and on again about once a second, for as long as the data is missing. The log shows the repeated timeouts.
  • A toggle needs the Head MCU. Without it, a silent hoverboard stays as it is.
  • ros2_control_node killed hard (SIGKILL) does not toggle. The motors are switched off by the start path instead (ADR 0011).

docs.title: The robot profile is the single source of facts about one physical Pilsbot
docs.text:
Before Humble the same facts lived in several places and disagreed. The wheelbase was 0.67 in the controller config and about 0.68 in the URDF. The serial ports were hardcoded in the driver. The steering calibration existed in four versions. Now pilsbot_description/profiles/<name>.yaml is the only place that holds them. Launch files take robot_profile:=<name or path> (default pilsbot) and read it through pilsbot_description.profile. The URDF reads it with xacro, and every other consumer gets its values from one of those two:

  • Geometry (wheelbase, front and rear track, wheel radius): the URDF, and the controller's wheel_base_distance, wheel_separation, and wheel_radius, which pilsbot.launch.py passes as a parameter file over the controller config.
  • Steering (mechanical limit, potentiometer calibration): the URDF joint limit, and the driver and head_mcu_node. The driver reads the calibration from its URDF hardware parameters.
  • Device ports (hoverboard, Head MCU, lighting board, gamepad by SDL index or name): the driver through its URDF hardware parameters, the lighting bridge, and joy_node.
  • Gamepad mapping: the name of the teleop config in pilsbot_driver/config.

A missing or invalid value stops the launch, or the driver's on_init, with a message that names it. No hardcoded fallback is used.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
The profile holds facts about the robot, not tuning. PIDs, speed and acceleration limits, and the controller's soft steering limit (1.45 rad, inside the mechanical 1.58) stay with the nodes that use them, because they change when behaviour is tuned, not when the robot is rebuilt.

Not in the profile yet:

  • The GNSS receiver: its port (/dev/ttyGPS) and frame are fixed in pilsbot_gnss_receiver's u-blox.yaml.
  • The simulation: acker_diff_controller_sim.yaml still carries its own copy of the geometry.

docs.title: Considered options
docs.text:
• The URDF as the single source: rejected. Launch files need ports and the gamepad mapping before any URDF exists, and those are not robot geometry.
  • Keep each value with its consumer and check them against each other in tests: rejected. That keeps four places to edit when the robot changes, and it only catches disagreements that someone thought to test.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Re-measuring the wheelbase is one edit, and it moves the URDF, the controller, and the legacy-log converter together. Logs converted earlier keep the old value (ADR 0002).
  • The SDL gamepad fields have no Foxy equivalent (ADR 0001).

docs.title: Kohlfahrt logs are split MCAP files on the SSD; Foxglove on the robot is read-only
docs.text:
The stack container records Kohlfahrt logs with pilsbot_bringup's log_kohl.launch.py, which kohlfahrt_teleop_and_log.launch.py starts next to the driving stack. The topics come from config/recording.yaml in groups (robot_state, logs, commands, gnss, camera), so a short test drive can leave the camera out with groups:=.... Recordings are MCAP without compression, split every 300 s:

  • MCAP: Foxglove opens it directly, a file cut off by a crash stays readable, and it is rosbag2's default in later distros (ADR 0006). The Foxy logs were SQLite.
  • No compression: camera frames are already JPEG from the OAK's encoder, and the Nano's CPU is needed elsewhere. Decoded images are never recorded.
  • Split files: a crash or a full disk loses at most one file. Humble's rosbag2 writes latched topics only into the first file, so static_data_republisher re-sends /tf_static and /robot_description every 10 s, and every file opens on its own.

Bags go to /workspaces/bags, the bind mount of the external SSD. The recorder does not start unless the marker file <output_dir>/.pilsbot_bags exists, which is created once on the SSD (README), or if less than min_free_gb (10 GB) is free there. Without the SSD it would fill the Nano's SD card, and a bind mount alone does not prove the SSD is there: the directory may exist on the root filesystem. check_output_dir:=false records anyway, with a warning. Bag names get a random suffix, because the Nano has no RTC and dates repeat after a reboot.

Recording never stops the robot. A refused output directory or a recorder that exits prints a !! banner, and driving continues.

foxglove_bridge runs in the stack container for live viewing (port 8765), with only the connectionGraph and assets capabilities, and a client topic whitelist that matches nothing. The bridge has no authentication. With its defaults, anyone on the network at a public outing could publish cmd_vel, switch controllers, or change parameters, which bypasses the enable button. foxglove_capabilities:=all (or a list) enables writing for development and prints a warning banner.

docs.title: Considered options
docs.text:
• Record the cameras in the camera container, next to the frames: rejected, also for the transition. The JPEG streams are small enough for DDS (about 4 MB/s, ADR 0004), and one recorder keeps one bag per outing.
  • Foxglove with the upstream defaults (all capabilities): rejected for the reason above. Development setups opt in explicitly.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Without the SSD mounted (no marker file), nothing is recorded. The launch output shows a NOT RECORDING banner.
  • Foxglove cannot publish, call services, or edit parameters by default. Its teleop and parameter panels stay inactive.
  • Live Foxglove clients see /robot_description again every 10 s while recording.
  • During the camera transition (ADR 0003) the camera group lists the topics of the Foxy camera container (pilsbot_bringup#7): /color/video/image/compressed, /color/video/camera_info, /image_raw/compressed, /camera_info. The compressed topics exist only if compressed_image_transport is in the Foxy camera image, which is still to be checked on the robot with ros2 topic list. Their JPEG is encoded on the Nano's CPU, not by the OAK. The group changes to the Humble camera node's names when that container moves to Humble.
  • New logs contain /dynamic_joint_states instead of /hoverboard_api and /head_mcu (ADR 0006), and /rosout in the logs group.

docs.title: systemd restarts the whole stack container, and the motors are switched off between runs
docs.text:
On the robot, pilsbot_stack.service from useful-scripts (Restart=always, RestartSec=1) runs startall.bash:

  1. enable_motors.bash sets the motor outputs of the I2C port expander.
  2. setup_serials.bash creates the device links /dev/ttyHoverboard, /dev/ttyHeadMCU, and /dev/ttyGPS.
  3. start_latest_pilsbot_stack.sh execs docker run --rm of the stack container, whose command execs ros2 launch pilsbot_bringup kohlfahrt_teleop_and_log.launch.py (Kohl mode).
  4. disable_motors.bash clears the motor outputs. A trap … EXIT runs it however startall.bash ends, including a failed step or a non-zero exit of the container (useful-scripts#2).

Inside the launch, nothing restarts ros2_control_node. If it exits, for any reason, the whole launch shuts down (OnProcessExit → Shutdown). The container then exits, the motors are switched off, and systemd starts everything again a second later with a fresh controller manager. Failures below that level are handled where they happen:

  • Hardware drop-outs: the hardware activator (ADR 0007).
  • Devices that are missing at startup or vanish later: the lighting bridge and the GNSS driver respawn every 5 s until their port is there.
  • A recorder that exits: a banner, and driving continues (ADR 0010).

The camera container is not part of this service. It drives nothing, so a camera failure must not restart the driving stack, and the stack restarting must not restart the cameras.

Container Builds Started by Stack src/ros2.repos in ~/pilsbot_humble_ws pilsbot_stack.service (target); by hand for now, see below Camera src/jetson-camera.repos (dustynv image, ADR 0003); during the transition the Foxy workspace as built by hand (README)

docs.title: Considered options
docs.text:
• respawn=True on ros2_control_node: rejected. The motors would stay enabled across the restart, and a restart loop would hide inside the launch output instead of showing in systemctl status.
  • A Docker restart policy on the container: rejected. It skips disable_motors.bash and enable_motors.bash and the serial setup.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• A crash of the controller manager costs a full stack restart of a few seconds plus the activator period, and the odometry restarts at the origin.
  • disable_motors.bash is the only thing that switches the motors off when ros2_control_node dies without its destructor running, for example on SIGKILL (ADR 0008).
  • Until the service starts the Humble image, it still runs the Foxy stack. The Humble stack container (pilsbot-humble) is started by hand with docker exec (README). In that setup an exit of ros2_control_node still shuts the launch down, but only the ros2 launch ends: the container stays up, nothing restarts, and the motors stay enabled. The tester runs disable_motors.bash by hand after stopping the container (README, "On the Jetson Nano", step 4).

docs.title: Pilsbot ROS2 Workspace
docs.text:
This repository contains a preconfigured workspace for development of the Pilsbot platform. The branch humble is the primary development line. The branch foxy is the maintained legacy line, which receives backports of substantial improvements (see docs/adr).

One branch serves every target. The targets differ only in which repos files they import and which devcontainer they use:

Target Devcontainer Repos files Desktop development and simulation .devcontainer/desktop src/ros2.repos, src/desktop.repos (default) Jetson Nano, everything except the camera .devcontainer/jetson-stack src/ros2.repos Jetson Nano, OAK camera with hardware decoding .devcontainer/jetson-camera src/jetson-camera.repos

The Nano runs two containers side by side; see ADR 0003. Project vocabulary lives in GLOSSARY.md.

docs.title: Deliberate differences from the Foxy line
docs.text:
The Humble line is not a plain port. On the robot it behaves differently from Foxy in these ways, all on purpose:

  • Startup: the hardware and the controllers come up inactive and are activated by the hardware activator, at least 5 s after the launch (ADR 0007).
  • Hoverboard power: the power toggle runs in the Head MCU thread instead of sleeping about 1 s in the control loop. It is never pressed after an error, only on 1 s of silence and on clean shutdown (ADR 0008). The driver measures its timeouts on the steady clock, not the system clock.
  • Lost Head MCU: the steering angle and endstops become NaN at once, and the driver reconnects once a second until the Head MCU is back. Before, the angle froze at its last value and the controller kept steering on it.
  • Controller stops:
  • NaN steering or wheel positions halt the wheels, and the speed ramps up from standstill afterwards.
  • A cmd_vel timeout (0.5 s) stops the wheels in the same cycle. Foxy ramped down at the acceleration limit, which took up to about 5 s from full speed.
  • The steering-error stop can now fire: linear speed goes to 0 while the steering angle is more than angle.z.max_angle_setpoint_diff (0.85 rad) from its setpoint and the steering loop has authority. On Foxy it compared the PID output and never fired.
  • Odometry: /odom and its TF are stamped with ROS time (Foxy: the steady clock), and they track base_footprint at the rear axle centre in odom (ADR 0002).
  • Sensor topics: /dynamic_joint_states replaces /hoverboard_api and /head_mcu (ADR 0006).
  • Supervision: if ros2_control_node exits, the whole launch ends and systemd restarts the stack with the motors switched off in between. The lighting bridge and the GNSS driver respawn every 5 s while their port is missing (ADR 0011).
  • Recording and Foxglove: Kohlfahrt logs are MCAP split every 300 s, nothing is recorded without the SSD, and Foxglove is read-only (ADR 0010).
  • Gamepad: Humble's SDL joy_node selects the gamepad by index or name from the robot profile (ADR 0009) and reads /dev/input/event*. The button and axis mapping is not yet checked against SDL.
  • Cameras: the stack starts no camera; the camera container does (ADR 0003). During the transition it runs the Foxy camera nodes unchanged (OAK rgb_stereo_node at 480p and 10 fps). After the move to Humble the OAK runs mjpeg_node (colour 1280×720 at 30 fps, ADR 0004), and the OAK's camera_info is not recorded.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
You should already have Docker and VSCode with the remote containers plugin installed on your system.

  • docker
  • vscode
  • vscode dev containers extension

docs.title: Open it in vscode
docs.text:
Clone the repository to a folder of your choice with

git clone https://github.com/pilsbot/pilsbot_vscode_ws.git

or via ssh

git clone git@github.com:pilsbot/pilsbot_vscode_ws.git

Now that you've cloned your repo onto your computer, you can open it in VSCode (File->Open Folder).

When you open it for the first time, you should see a little popup that asks you if you would like to open it in a container. Say yes!

If you don't see the pop-up, click on the little green square in the bottom left corner, which should bring up the container dialog

In the dialog, select "Dev Containers: Reopen in Container" and pick the configuration for your target

VSCode will build the dockerfile inside of .devcontainer for you. If you open a terminal inside VSCode (Terminal->New Terminal), you should see that your username has been changed to ros, and the bottom left green corner should say "Dev Container"

docs.title: Setup the workspace
docs.text:
1. Import the sources and install their dependencies with ./import_sources.sh (desktop default), or pass the repos files for your target, e.g. ./import_sources.sh src/ros2.repos. The tasks Terminal->Run Task..->setup and import from workspace file do the same and ask for the target.
  2. Run the build task with Ctrl+Shift+B, or ./build.sh. Set BUILD_TYPE to override the default RelWithDebInfo.

docs.title: Check the build
docs.text:
The simulation (pilsbot_simulation) is not ported to Humble yet, so it is no smoke test for now. Check the build instead:

source install/setup.bash
ros2 pkg executables pilsbot_driver   # lists hardware_activator
xacro $(ros2 pkg prefix pilsbot_description)/share/pilsbot_description/urdf/pilsbot.urdf.xacro > /dev/null

./build.sh passes extra arguments to colcon build, e.g. ./build.sh --packages-select pilsbot_driver or ./build.sh --packages-skip <name>.

If any issues occur during the setup process, do not hesitate to open an issue, so we can fix the problem as soon as possible.

docs.title: On the Jetson Nano
docs.text: The Humble stack container lives next to the Foxy stack, which stays as it is: Foxy in ~/pilsbot_vscode_ws (container pilsbot_stack, started by pilsbot_stack.service from useful-scripts), Humble in a second workspace ~/pilsbot_humble_ws with the image pilsbot/humble-stack and the container pilsbot-humble. Never run both stacks at the same time: both drive the same serial ports, I2C port expander and gamepad.

docs.title: Build the image
docs.text:
JetPack 4.6 ships an old Docker whose seccomp profile does not know clone3, which Ubuntu 22.04 uses. docker run works around it with --security-opt seccomp=unconfined, but docker build cannot, so RUN apt-get update may fail while building. Check the Docker version on the Nano first:

docker version --format '{{.Server.Version}}'
  • 20.10.10 or newer: build on the Nano.

git clone -b humble https://github.com/pilsbot/pilsbot_vscode_ws.git ~/pilsbot_humble_ws cd ~/pilsbot_humble_ws docker build -t pilsbot/humble-stack \ --build-arg WORKSPACE=/workspaces/pilsbot_humble_ws .devcontainer/jetson-stack

Add --build-arg USER_UID=$(id -u) if id -u is not 1000. - Older, or the build fails with clone3, Operation not permitted or pthread_create errors: build for arm64 on a desktop (about 4 minutes under qemu) and copy the image over.

docker run --privileged --rm tonistiigi/binfmt --install arm64 # once, enables qemu docker buildx build --platform linux/arm64 --load -t pilsbot/humble-stack \ --build-arg WORKSPACE=/workspaces/pilsbot_humble_ws .devcontainer/jetson-stack docker save pilsbot/humble-stack | ssh pilsbot@<nano> docker load

docs.title: Start the container
docs.text:
The Foxy service also prepares the hardware: its startall.bash runs enable_motors.bash (switches the motor power on through the MCP23017 port expander at I2C 0x20), setup_serials.bash (stops serial-getty and creates /dev/ttyHoverboard, /dev/ttyHeadMCU and /dev/ttyGPS), the Foxy container, and disable_motors.bash when the container exits. The Humble container does none of this, so on the Nano run, in this order:

# 1. Stop Foxy. `stop` lasts until the next reboot only: the service is enabled and
#    starts Foxy again at boot. After a reboot, stop it again before starting Humble.
sudo systemctl stop pilsbot_stack
docker ps                                   # must not list pilsbot_stack

# 2. Prepare the hardware like the service does (the symlinks in /dev do not survive a reboot)
bash ~/useful-scripts/setup_serials.bash    # calls sudo itself; at the end, ttyHeadMCU and ttyGPS must point to devices
sudo ~/useful-scripts/enable_motors.bash

# 3. Start the Humble container (first time; later `docker start pilsbot-humble`)
docker run -d --name pilsbot-humble --network=host --ipc=host --privileged \
  --security-opt seccomp=unconfined --security-opt apparmor=unconfined \
  --group-add "$(getent group input | cut -d: -f3)" \
  --group-add "$(getent group i2c | cut -d: -f3)" \
  -v /dev:/dev -v /run/udev:/run/udev:ro \
  -v ~/pilsbot_humble_ws:/workspaces/pilsbot_humble_ws \
  --mount type=bind,source=/media/externSSD/bags,target=/workspaces/bags \
  -e ROS_LOG_DIR=/workspaces/pilsbot_humble_ws/log/ros \
  -u ros -w /workspaces/pilsbot_humble_ws pilsbot/humble-stack sleep infinity
docker exec -it pilsbot-humble bash
./import_sources.sh src/ros2.repos
MAKEFLAGS=-j1 ./build.sh --parallel-workers 1   # the 4 GB Nano runs out of memory otherwise

# 4. When done testing: stop the container, then switch the motors off
docker stop pilsbot-humble
sudo ~/useful-scripts/disable_motors.bash

~/useful-scripts is /home/pilsbot/useful-scripts, where pilsbot_stack.service expects it. To return to Foxy without a reboot: sudo systemctl start pilsbot_stack. Do not systemctl disable the service for a test; a reboot is the way back to the normal Foxy robot. The Humble container has no --restart policy, so after a reboot only Foxy runs.

Why the flags:

  • --group-add: --privileged lets the container open devices, but the user ros still needs file permissions. Humble's joy_node (SDL) reads the gamepad from /dev/input/event* (root:input, mode 0660), Foxy read the world-readable /dev/input/js0. The port expander uses /dev/i2c-* (group i2c). The gids must be the host's, which differ from the image's, so they are looked up on the host. Check that both getent calls print a line; ls -ln /dev/input/event* /dev/i2c-* shows the gids the devices really use.
  • -v /run/udev:/run/udev:ro: SDL learns about gamepads that connect later through udev.
  • --mount instead of -v for the bags: it fails if /media/externSSD/bags does not exist, where -v would create it. That does not prove the SSD is mounted: the Foxy service binds the same path with --volume, so if Foxy ever started without the SSD, the directory exists on the root file system and --mount binds it. The real guard is in the recording launch (log_kohl.launch.py, pilsbot_bringup): it records only if <output_dir>/.pilsbot_bags exists. Create that marker once, with the SSD mounted:

mountpoint /media/externSSD && sudo touch /media/externSSD/bags/.pilsbot_bags

Without the SSD, the recording launch prints a NOT RECORDING banner and the rest of the stack runs. To record elsewhere, create the marker in that directory and bind it instead.

The VS Code devcontainer .devcontainer/jetson-stack uses the same flags, and needs the same steps 1, 2 and 4 on the host. For --group-add it reads PILSBOT_INPUT_GID and PILSBOT_I2C_GID from the environment of the VS Code process that opens the container. Export them, then start VS Code from that shell (close other VS Code windows first, or the running instance keeps its old environment):

export PILSBOT_INPUT_GID=$(getent group input | cut -d: -f3)
export PILSBOT_I2C_GID=$(getent group i2c | cut -d: -f3)
code ~/pilsbot_humble_ws

If they are unset, the devcontainer falls back to the group names input and i2c, which resolve to the image's own groups. ros is already in those, so nothing is granted and the gamepad and I2C fail with "Permission denied". Check inside the container: id must list the two host gids.

The camera container (.devcontainer/jetson-camera) runs as root, not ros, so it needs no group settings. It records nothing and does not mount the bags.

docs.title: DDS
docs.text:
Both containers use CycloneDDS (RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=rmw_cyclonedds_cpp) on the host network, and must use the same ROS_DOMAIN_ID (default 0; set it with -e ROS_DOMAIN_ID=<n> in both, and on a laptop that runs ros2 commands against the robot). Foxglove connects over its WebSocket (port 8765) and does not depend on DDS.

The Nano has several network interfaces (docker0, l4tbr0, wlan0, ...), and CycloneDDS may pick one the laptop cannot reach. If ros2 topic list on the laptop sees nothing from the robot, pin the interface with the shipped config by adding to docker run:

-e CYCLONEDDS_URI=file:///workspaces/pilsbot_humble_ws/.devcontainer/jetson-stack/cyclonedds.xml \
-e PILSBOT_DDS_INTERFACE=wlan0

Take the interface name from ip -br addr on the Nano. Before using it, know what it costs:

  • CycloneDDS refuses to start a node when the named interface does not exist, and probably also when it has no IP address (wifi not connected, no access point on an outing). Then no node starts, the driver included, so the robot does not drive.
  • The camera container must use the same setting (the same two variables, with the path to cyclonedds.xml in its workspace). If one container is pinned and the other is not, they may pick different interfaces and not see each other's topics.

So leave it off for outings, and use it only when the laptop really cannot see the robot.

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text: • all packages added to the workspace should use https. If you have a Github account logged in your VSCode installation, you can easily push without the need for password authentication. You will be asked to acknowledge your login once via your browser and you're good to go.

docs.title: Cameras on the Nano during the transition
docs.text:
On Humble, the stack container starts no camera (kohlfahrt_teleop_and_log neither): the cameras belong to the camera container (ADR 0003). Until that container moves to the dustynv Humble image (.devcontainer/jetson-camera, src/jetson-camera.repos), it runs on Foxy:

  • Workspace: the Foxy workspace ~/pilsbot_vscode_ws as the Foxy stack built it (pilsbot_depthai on foxy-devel, jetson_camera on master). Nothing is checked out or rebuilt, so the Foxy stack stays as it is.
  • Image: the one pilsbot_stack.service uses, named in container= in ~/useful-scripts/start_latest_pilsbot_stack.sh.
  • Launch: the Foxy pilsbot_bringup has no camera.launch.py, so the container starts the two camera launches directly, with the settings of the Foxy Kohl mode (OAK-D Lite, 480p at 10 fps). publish_urdf:=false, because the Humble stack already publishes the OAK's frames from pilsbot_description.

Run it next to the Humble stack container pilsbot-humble, never next to the Foxy stack, which starts the same cameras itself (sudo systemctl stop pilsbot_stack first):

FOXY_IMAGE=$(sed -n 's/^container=//p' ~/useful-scripts/start_latest_pilsbot_stack.sh)
docker run -d --name pilsbot-camera --privileged --user ros --gpus=all \
  --network=host --cap-add=SYS_PTRACE \
  --security-opt=seccomp:unconfined --security-opt=apparmor:unconfined \
  -v /tmp/argus_socket:/tmp/argus_socket -v /dev:/dev \
  -v /home/pilsbot/pilsbot_vscode_ws:/workspaces/pilsbot_vscode_ws \
  "$FOXY_IMAGE" bash -c '
    trap "kill -INT \$(jobs -p)" INT TERM   # docker stop: shut both launches down cleanly
    . /workspaces/pilsbot_vscode_ws/install/local_setup.bash
    ros2 launch pilsbot_depthai rgb_stereo_node.launch.py camera_model:=OAK-D-LITE \
      colorResolution:=480p colorFramerate:=10 monoResolution:=480p monoFramerate:=10 \
      publish_urdf:=false &
    ros2 launch jetson_camera jetson_camera_launch.py &
    wait; wait'
docker logs -f pilsbot-camera                          # Ctrl+C leaves it running
docker stop -t 30 pilsbot-camera && docker rm pilsbot-camera

Check from pilsbot-humble with ros2 topic list that the camera topics arrive. Foxy and Humble talk over DDS for these message types (ADR 0003). Both containers must use the same ROS_DOMAIN_ID.

During the transition, the camera group of the Humble recording.yaml lists the Foxy camera topics (pilsbot_bringup#7), so log_kohl.launch.py with the camera group records them from the Humble stack container:

  • /color/video/image/compressed and /color/video/camera_info (OAK)
  • /image_raw/compressed and /camera_info (CSI camera)

The two compressed topics exist only if compressed_image_transport is installed in the Foxy camera image. Check on the robot, with the camera container running: ros2 topic list | grep -E 'compressed|camera_info' in pilsbot-humble. If the compressed topics are missing, the bags hold only the camera_info topics. The compressed plugin encodes JPEG on the camera container's CPU, only while the recorder subscribes; raw images and depth are not recorded. When the camera container moves to Humble, the group changes to the Humble camera node's names.

docs.title: Pilsbot
docs.text: Pilsbot is a hobby sidewalk robot on a hoverboard drivetrain with a passively steered front axle. This glossary covers the whole workspace, including the robot, its software lines, and its recorded data.

docs.title: Vehicle
docs.text:
Front axle: The steerable axle that carries the two driven hoverboard wheels and pivots relative to the chassis. Avoid: steering axle (when meaning the whole axle), drive axle

Rear axle: The rigid, unpowered axle fixed to the chassis.

Rear axle centre: The midpoint of the rear axle, which is the robot's reference point for pose, odometry, and planning. Avoid: base (unqualified), robot origin

Wheelbase: The distance from the front axle's pivot to the rear axle centre.

Steering angle: The angle between the front axle and the chassis, measured at the pivot. Avoid: steering position, pot value (for the calibrated angle)

Steering rate: How fast the steering angle changes. Avoid: steering angle velocity (ambiguous, see steering authority)

Steering authority: How strongly the controller actively turns the front axle towards the commanded steering angle; zero means passive steering only. The gamepad mappings and Ackermann commands carry it in the field steering_angle_velocity. Avoid: steering angle velocity (ambiguous, see steering rate)

Passive steering: Turning the front axle by driving its two wheels at different speeds, since no motor acts on the pivot.

Acker-diff steering: Pilsbot's drive scheme, which accepts Ackermann commands (speed and steering angle) and realises them through passive steering. Avoid: diff drive, Ackermann drive (alone)

Endstop: A switch marking the mechanical limit of the steering angle on either side.

Hoverboard: The repurposed hoverboard controller board and its two hub-motor wheels, which together drive the front axle.

Head MCU: The microcontroller on the front axle that reads the steering potentiometer and the endstops, and presses the hoverboard's power button.

Power toggle: One simulated press of the hoverboard's power button, which switches the hoverboard on if it is off and off if it is on; nobody can tell which beforehand. Avoid: power on, power off, switching on (for the press itself)

Hardware activator: The node that brings the Pilsbot hardware and its controllers into operation whenever they are not, at startup and after every drop-out. Avoid: watchdog, supervisor

Enable button: The gamepad button that must be held for teleop to drive the robot; releasing it stops the robot (dead-man switch). Avoid: deadman, safety button

Turbo button: The gamepad button that drives with the faster turbo scaling while held, with or without the enable button; releasing it stops the robot like the enable button. Avoid: snail button

Robot profile: The single description of one physical Pilsbot: geometry, steering calibration, the ports of its devices, and its gamepad mapping. The GNSS receiver is not in it yet (ADR 0009). Avoid: config, robot yaml

StVO lighting: Headlight, turn signal, brake, and hazard behaviour that follows German road traffic rules (StVO). Avoid: indicators (for the whole set), LEDs

docs.title: Perception
docs.text:
OAK: The OAK-D Lite camera, which provides colour, stereo depth, and on-camera neural inference. Avoid: depthai (for the device), Luxonis camera

Drivability map: A robot-local map that labels the ground ahead as drivable sidewalk, road, or not drivable. Avoid: costmap (for the semantic layer), segmentation map

docs.title: Software lines
docs.text:
Humble line: The primary development line of all Pilsbot repositories, targeting ROS 2 Humble.

Foxy line: The maintained legacy line targeting ROS 2 Foxy, which receives backports of substantial distro-independent improvements. Avoid: old branch, foxy-devel

Camera container: The Nano container with Jetson L4T libraries that owns both cameras: the OAK with its hardware-accelerated decoding, and the CSI camera.

Stack container: The Nano container that runs everything else from Humble binary packages.

docs.title: Frames
docs.text:
odom: The world-fixed odometry frame, whose origin is where the front axle stood when odometry was last reset. Avoid: odom_raw

base_footprint: The rear axle centre on the ground, which is the frame odometry tracks in odom. Avoid: base_link (for the tracked frame)

base_link: The rear axle centre at wheel-axle height, one wheel radius above base_footprint.

docs.title: Data
docs.text:
Kohlfahrt: A real outing with the robot, usually in public. Avoid: test drive (for an outing)

Kohl mode: The robot's configuration for a Kohlfahrt: the stack with gamepad teleop and recording, and the cameras at a reduced data rate (OAK at 480p and 10 fps on the Foxy line).

Kohlfahrt log: A bag recorded during a Kohlfahrt, used as raw material for datasets.

Legacy log: A Kohlfahrt log recorded before the robot reference point moved to the rear axle centre, which must go through the legacy-log converter before it is used with current frames.

Legacy-log converter: The tool that turns a legacy log into a Kohlfahrt log with current frames and topics. Avoid: bag migration, re-rooting (for the whole tool)
